fullPassage: Imagine you live in a small village where you and three other villagers depend on the local fish pond for food. The pond starts off with a dozen fish, and for every two fish, one baby is added each night. So, to maximize your supply of food, how many fish should you catch each day? Assume baby fish grow to full size immediately, the pond begins at full capacity, and ignore the sex of the fish. The answer? One, and not just you: every villager's food supply is maximized when each fisherman takes one fish a day. Here's the math: if each villager takes one fish, eight are left overnight. Each pair produces one baby, so the next day the pond is fully restocked with twelve. If anyone takes more than one, the number of reproductive pairs drops, and the population can't bounce back. Eventually the fish are gone and all four villagers starve. This pond is one example of a classic problem called the tragedy of the commons. It was first described in an 1833 pamphlet by economist William Forster Lloyd, on the overgrazing of cattle on village common areas. More than 100 years later, ecologist Garrett Hardin revived it to describe what happens when many individuals share a limited resource: grazing land, fishing areas, living space, even clean air. Hardin said that in these situations, people want what is good for themselves today, but that hurts everyone later. Nobody wins. We get too much grazing, too much fishing, too many people, and too much pollution. The key feature is that an individual can benefit himself while spreading the negative effects across the larger population. Let's look at our fish pond again. Each fisherman is motivated to take as many fish as he can, while any decline in reproduction is shared by the whole village. Anxious not to lose out, he concludes it's in his best interest to take an extra fish, or two, or three. But the other fishermen reach the same conclusion, and that's the tragedy. Optimizing for the self in the short term isn't optimal for anyone in the long term. The fish pond is a simple example, but the same thing really happens in the world around us. A coal-fired power plant gives customers cheap electricity and owners profit; these local benefits help in the short term, but the pollution spreads across the entire atmosphere and lasts thousands of years. Other examples include littering, water shortages, deforestation, traffic jams, even buying bottled water. But human civilization has proven capable of something remarkable. We form social contracts, make communal agreements, elect governments, and pass laws to save our collective selves from our own individual impulses. It isn't easy, and we don't always get it right. But at our best we have shown that we can solve these problems, and can continue to if we remember Hardin's lesson: When the tragedy of the commons applies, what's good for all of us is good for each of us.
